parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle High German urohse, composed of ur (“aurochs”) (from Old High German ūro, from Proto-West Germanic *ūr) + ohse (“ox”) (modern Ochse).

From Northern Old French berfroi (“movable siege tower”), from Middle High German bercfrit (“protecting shelter”, literally “that which watches over peace”), from bergen (“to protect”) + frid (“peace”).
From Middle High German bleichvar (“pale-coloured”), from bleich (“pale”) + var (“colour”) (compare German Farbe).

parole.significato: to sift, to sieve, especially the flour from the bran

Inherited from Middle French bride, from Old French bride (“rein, bridle”), from Middle High German brīdel (“rein, bridle”), from Old High German brīdil (“rein, bridle”) (compare also Old High German brittil (“rein, strap”), French bretelle), from Proto-West Germanic *brigdil (“bridle”). Compare Spa

Borrowed from Middle High German chouch (“jackdaw”), from Old High German kaha, from Proto-West Germanic *kahu (“jackdaw”), ultimately imitative; related to English chough, Portuguese chuca, Dutch kauw, Swedish kaja. More at chough.
Calque of Middle High German engellisches horn (“angelic horn”), by misunderstanding.

parole.significato: jack (device for raising and supporting a heavy object)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French cric, from Middle High German kriec (“jack, winch”). Of uncertain further origin, but supposed to be from the adjective kriege (“recalcitrant”), which is related with kriec (“war”). The last noun can hardly be the direct origin, although the word first occurs mostly in m

parole.significato: foeder (large barrel used for aging beer or wine)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle High German vuoder, from Old High German fuodar, from Proto-West Germanic *fōþr. Cognate with English fother, German Fuder, Dutch voer, voeder, etc.

Inherited from Middle French hutte, from Old French hute (“hut”), from Middle High German hütte, from Old High German hutta (“hut”), from Proto-Germanic *hudjǭ (“hut, shelter”), from *hūdijaną (“to conceal”), related to Old English hȳdan (“to hide”). More at hut, hide.
Inherited from Middle French quille, borrowed from Middle High German kegel, from Old High German kegil, from Proto-West Germanic *kagil (“pile, stake, peg, cone”).

parole.significato: the slatted side of a truck, carriage etc.
parole.testo: From Middle High German reidel, from or related to Old High German ridan (“to turn”).
Inherited from Old French rote, Middle High German rotte.

Inherited from Middle French trinquer (ca. 1400), from Middle High German trinken, from Old High German trinkan, from Proto-West Germanic *drinkan, from Proto-Germanic *drinkaną. Cognate with English drink.
